unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 1 asks what stories are for. You read “The Camel and the Sparrow”, a fable in which a boastful camel learns that the smallest helper found the water, and “The Silence After the Rumble”, in which Amal sweeps the steps of a courthouse in a town rebuilding after an earthquake. Alongside them you meet twenty-five new words and the adjective and preposition pairs that make feelings precise, such as proud of, anxious about and grateful for. The unit ends with a fable of your own, planned, drafted and revised.
unit.learningPath: Start with the two information texts on fables and folklore. Read the fable, then the two parts of the story. Answer the comprehension questions and work through the vocabulary activities. Study the six grammar sections on adjective and preposition pairs. Speak, then plan, draft and revise your own fable. Finish with the checkpoint quiz and the self-assessment.
howToUse: Read in this order: the two information texts, “What Makes a Fable?” and “Folklore Around the World”; then the fable “The Camel and the Sparrow”; then “The Silence After the Rumble”, parts 1 and 2. Each text builds on the one before, and Comprehension asks about all five.
The story continues in later units, so read both parts closely.
The six writing tasks build one piece: you plan your own fable, draft it, then check and improve it — do them in order.

readings.title: What Makes a Fable?
readings.passageScript:
A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson, and that lesson is called the moral.
Most fables use animal characters who talk, think and feel exactly as people do. Writers call this anthropomorphism, which simply means giving human qualities to an animal.
A fable is deliberately short. It does not describe every room or every hour of the day. It tells one problem quickly, so that nothing distracts you from the lesson at the end.
Each animal usually stands for one clear human quality. A fox is clever, a tortoise is patient, a lion is proud. Because the character carries only one strong trait, you can see the moral much more easily.
Here is a checklist you can use with any fable you read.
Animal characters who speak and behave like people.
A short, simple plot built around one clear problem.
A conflict that the characters must face and solve.
A moral at the end that states the lesson plainly.
Animals that stand for a single human quality.
Fables are not the same as novels or fairy tales. A novel has room for many characters and many years. A fairy tale can wander into magic for pages at a time. A fable strips everything away until only the lesson is left standing.
When you read the fable in this unit, keep a pencil beside you. Note what each animal says, note what each animal does, and then decide whether the moral matches their behaviour.

readings.title: Folklore Around the World
readings.passageScript:
Folklore means the traditional stories, beliefs and customs that a group of people share and pass on.
Every culture has folklore, and most of it was spoken aloud long before anybody wrote it down.
In East Africa, families gather in the evening while an older relative tells a tale everybody knows.
Somali storytellers call these tales sheeko. A sheeko might teach generosity, or courage, or respect for the people who raised you.
Aesop’s fables come from ancient Greece, and two of them, “The Tortoise and the Hare” and “The Boy Who Cried Wolf”, are known almost everywhere.
West African storytellers tell Anansi tales. In them a clever spider talks his way out of trouble that he caused himself.
The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection about animals who learn hard lessons about friendship, trust and leadership.
These traditions grew up thousands of miles apart. Yet every one of them chose the same tool: a short story with a lesson inside it.
That is why this unit is called “There is a lesson in that”. Wherever people live, they teach one another through stories.
Ask an older person in your family for a tale they were told as a child. You are collecting folklore when you do.

readings.title: The Camel and the Sparrow
readings.setting: A village at the edge of a great desert
readings.passageScript:
At the edge of a great desert lived a tall camel named Jamal. Beside him lived a tiny sparrow named Zara.
They shared the same region, close to a village of low houses ringed by thorn trees and golden sand.
The villagers looked after one another, exactly as their ancestors had done for many generations before them.
One morning a fierce sandstorm swept across the village. It roared and rumbled for hours and filled the air with dust.
When the misty dawn came, the people stepped outside and found their homes in rubble. Walls had crumbled and roofs had blown away.
Worst of all, the well lay buried under deep sand. The village elder called everybody together beneath the tallest tree.
“We must rebuild,” she said firmly, “and every creature here has a role to play.”
Jamal stepped forward proudly. “I am the strongest,” he declared. “I will carry the heavy stones and drag the timber.”
He hauled great rocks on his broad back while the villagers cheered. Jamal was very proud of his own strength.
Zara fluttered down and landed on a branch beside him. “I want to help too,” she chirped. “What can I do?”
Jamal laughed loudly. “You? You are far too small. Sit on your branch and sing. Leave the real work to those of us who are strong.”
Zara felt a wave of anxiety. Perhaps the camel was right. Perhaps she was simply too small to matter at all.
Then she remembered what her grandmother once told her: “Even the smallest raindrop helps to fill the river.”
So Zara flew higher than any camel could ever reach. From up there she saw what nobody on the ground could see.
A thin green line lay far to the east, behind a ridge of rocks. It was a hidden stream, and the village needed water for survival.
She swooped down to the elder. “There is water beyond the eastern ridge!” she cried. “I can see it from the sky!”
Workers walked out to the ridge and found the stream exactly where Zara had described it. Clean water reached the village that same day.
That evening the elder gathered everybody under the stars. “Jamal carried our stones, and we are grateful for his strength,” she said.
“But Zara found our water, and she saved us from thirst. Strength is noble, and so is the wisdom to see what others cannot.”
Jamal lowered his great head. “I was wrong,” he said softly. “You were not too small. You were exactly the right size for the right job.”
Zara smiled at him. “Every creature has a role,” she said. “We only have to find out what ours is.”
Moral: no contribution is too small, because everybody has something important to offer.

readings.title: The Silence After the Rumble, part 1
readings.setting: A courthouse in a town rebuilding after an earthquake
readings.passageScript:
The courthouse was the only building still standing in the middle of the broken town.
All around it lay nothing but rubble. Walls had fallen. Roads had cracked. Yet one room, the courtroom, still held its shape.
Amal lived in a small residence nearby with her grandmother. Two years earlier an earthquake had shaken the whole valley.
Many families lost their homes that night, and others moved away to different regions of the country.
Amal and Grandma Hana stayed. “This is where your ancestor planted trees and built the first houses,” Grandma Hana said. “It is our place.”
Amal walked to the courthouse every single morning. Her role was simple: sweep the steps and fill the water jug on the judge’s bench.
It was not a large job, but it made her proud of herself. She did it carefully every day.
She always checked the door hinges, which were still bent from the night the ground moved. Some people said the building would fall soon.
To Amal it was the most important building in the town. It was where the town decided what was fair.
One misty morning Amal arrived early. The courtroom was completely silent. Then a deep rumble ran through the floor and she froze.
“Is the ground shaking again?” she whispered. It was not. A delivery lorry had passed too close to the damaged road.
Amal breathed out slowly and climbed the steps with her broom.
That day a visiting elder came to speak to the town’s students about justice and the law.
“When I was a boy,” he said, “we followed continental rules that outsiders had brought here. Now we shape our own laws instead.”
A boy near the front asked, “What happens if somebody breaks those laws?”
The elder answered, “The law must help people, never hurt them. A nation is measured by how it treats its smallest citizen.”
Amal listened hard. She felt a strange anxiety rising in her chest, the kind that grows just before you speak.
She raised her hand anyway. “Do I have a role?” she asked softly. “I only sweep the steps.”
The elder looked at her kindly. “Of course you do. You open the court. Without you, justice starts late. Never doubt your part.”

readings.title: The Silence After the Rumble, part 2
readings.setting: A courtroom trial and the walk home afterwards
readings.passageScript:
Later that week a trial began. A trader was accused of hiding emergency food that had been sent for the town’s children.
The courtroom was full. Amal stood near the back beside a woman in a silvery shawl. The woman had travelled from an urban centre far away.
“My son was ill after the earthquake,” the woman whispered. “There was no nutrition for him. If that man hid food, it cost lives.”
The judge entered and everybody sat down. The accused man shuffled to the front, holding a folded paper in his pouch.
Witnesses spoke one after another. Some voices shook badly. Others were slow and clear while the speakers searched their memories.
Then a boy of eleven walked forward. “I saw him,” he said. “He hid boxes behind the artificial wall in the storehouse.”
Somebody behind Amal whispered, “What is different about this trial?” Amal knew the answer at once: survival.
This time ordinary people had spoken out loud, and this time the court had real power to act.
The trader was found guilty. “The court will make sure the food is returned,” the judge said. “Families in rural villages need it most.”
Outside, the sun had dipped low. A pot of tea boiled on a coal stove in the courtyard.
Women from different regions shared small cups and talked quietly about the verdict.
One of them turned to Amal. “You come to every single trial,” she said. “Why?”
“I want to understand how nations work,” Amal answered. “How laws are made, and what justice actually means.”
The woman smiled. “You might make a noble lawyer one day.”
Amal laughed. “Maybe. But I like being early. I like unlocking the doors. It feels like opening a promise.”
That evening she walked home past cracked walls and empty plots where shops had once stood.
From far away she heard a soft rumble, but this time it was only thunder. The sky hung grey and misty above her.
At home Grandma Hana stirred soup over the fire. “The road may be cracked,” she said, “but we walk it anyway.”
Later Amal encountered Theo, the neighbours’ boy, who had come to ask Grandma Hana about a land document.
“Do you work at the court?” he asked. Amal paused. “Actually, I do,” she said. “I unlock the doors.”
Theo looked at her as though she were important, and at last Amal believed it herself.

comprehension.question: In “What Makes a Fable?”, what name is given to the lesson at the end of a fable?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The lesson at the end of a fable is called the moral.
comprehension.explanation: The opening sentence states it directly: a fable teaches a lesson, and that lesson is called the moral.

comprehension.question: The text uses the word anthropomorphism. What does a writer do when they use it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They give human qualities to an animal, so it talks, thinks and feels as a person does.
comprehension.explanation: The second paragraph defines the word for the reader as giving human qualities to an animal.

comprehension.question: Which two fables by Aesop does “Folklore Around the World” name?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It names “The Tortoise and the Hare” and “The Boy Who Cried Wolf”.
comprehension.explanation: Both titles appear in the sentence about ancient Greece, where the text calls them known almost everywhere.

comprehension.question: The traditions in this text grew up thousands of miles apart. What did all of them choose to do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They all chose to teach through a short story with a lesson folded inside it.
comprehension.explanation: The closing paragraphs draw the four traditions together and name the shared tool as the short story with a lesson.

comprehension.question: In “The Camel and the Sparrow”, what did the villagers find when the misty dawn came after the sandstorm?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They found their homes in rubble, with walls crumbled, roofs blown away and the well buried under sand.
comprehension.explanation: The paragraph after the sandstorm lists the damage in order: crumbled walls, missing roofs, then the buried well.

comprehension.question: How does Zara feel when Jamal laughs at her, and which words in the fable show it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She feels a wave of anxiety, and the fable says she wondered whether she was simply too small to matter.
comprehension.explanation: The text names the feeling as anxiety and then shows the thought behind it, which is stronger evidence than the label alone.

comprehension.question: Why could Zara find the hidden stream when nobody on the ground could?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She flew higher than any camel could reach, so from the sky she saw the thin green line behind the ridge.
comprehension.explanation: The fable links her height to her discovery: from up there she saw what nobody on the ground could see.

comprehension.question: The elder says that strength is noble and so is wisdom. How does that line prepare the reader for the moral?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It gives both animals real value, so the moral that no contribution is too small feels earned rather than sudden.

comprehension.question: In part 1 of “The Silence After the Rumble”, what two jobs did Amal do at the courthouse each morning?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She swept the steps and filled the water jug on the judge’s bench.
comprehension.explanation: Her role is described in one sentence, and both tasks sit side by side in it.

comprehension.question: Why does Amal freeze when she hears the deep rumble in the empty courtroom?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She thinks the ground is shaking again, because an earthquake had damaged the town two years earlier.

comprehension.question: In part 2, what evidence did the boy of eleven give at the trial?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He said he had seen the trader hide boxes behind the artificial wall in the storehouse.
comprehension.explanation: The boy gives the only direct eyewitness account in the trial, and he names the exact hiding place.

comprehension.correctAnswer: She now counts unlocking the doors as real work at the court, so she claims her role instead of shrinking it.

grammar.title: What Are Adjectives + Prepositions?
grammar.explanation: An adjective describes a noun or a pronoun by naming a quality, a feeling or an opinion. After a verb, many adjectives cannot stand alone, so they reach forward to a preposition to finish the idea.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
An adjective describes a noun or a pronoun: proud, anxious, afraid, excited, interested, good, sorry, angry, kind, grateful, jealous, keen.
A preposition is a small linking word: of, about, in, at, for, with, to, on.
After a verb such as “is” or “was”, many adjectives need a preposition before the noun that completes them.
Pattern: subject + verb + adjective + preposition + noun.
Jamal was proud of his own strength.
Zara felt anxious about being too small.
The villagers were grateful for the hidden stream.
Take the preposition away and the sentence breaks. “I am proud my work” is incomplete, because “of” is the word that joins “proud” to “my work”.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often drop the linking word altogether and write “She was proud her team.” Put the preposition back and the sentence closes properly: “She was proud of her team.”
grammar.memoryTip: Say the adjective aloud and listen for the gap after it. If your voice wants to keep going, a preposition belongs in that gap.

Two of these sentences are missing their preposition. Find them and write them out correctly. | Nora is good at drawing birds. | Leo was sorry the broken window. | Sami is keen on football. | Maya was jealous her friend's new bicycle.

Check yourself: Part A: 1. grateful – for. 2. anxious – about. 3. interested – in. Part B: the two sentences missing their preposition are “Leo was sorry the broken window” and “Maya was jealous her friend's new bicycle.” Corrected: “Leo was sorry for the broken window.” and “Maya was jealous of her friend's new bicycle.”

grammar.title: How to Use Adjectives + Prepositions
grammar.explanation: Four steps turn a bare adjective into a complete idea: find the adjective, choose its partner preposition, add what comes next, then build the whole sentence around it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Step 1. Find the describing word. In “Amal felt anxious”, the adjective is anxious.
Step 2. Choose its partner preposition. Anxious takes about.
Step 3. Add the noun, pronoun or idea that completes the meaning: anxious about the journey.
Step 4. Build the full sentence with a subject and a verb: “Amal was anxious about the journey.”
Learn these fifteen pairs by heart.
proud of — She was proud of her team.
anxious about — He was anxious about the exam.
interested in — I am interested in history.
good at — She is good at running.
bad at — I am bad at cooking.
afraid of — The child was afraid of the storm.
excited about — They were excited about the trip.
sorry for — I am sorry for the mistake.
angry with — She was angry with her brother.
kind to — Always be kind to others.
responsible for — He is responsible for the garden.
jealous of — She was jealous of her friend.
grateful for — We are grateful for your help.
worried about — Mum is worried about the weather.
keen on — I am keen on football.
grammar.commonMistake: It is tempting to guess the preposition from the meaning, so learners write “She is good in maths.” Good always takes at: “She is good at maths.”

grammar.title: Adjectives with More Than One Preposition
grammar.explanation: A few adjectives keep two partners, and the one you pick changes the meaning of the sentence. Angry, sorry and grateful are the three you will meet most often.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
angry with a person: “She was angry with her friend.”
angry about a situation: “She was angry about the decision.”
sorry for somebody you feel sympathy towards: “I am sorry for the family who lost their shop.”
sorry about something you did yourself: “I am sorry about the mess.”
grateful for a thing you were given: “I am grateful for the food.”
grateful to the person who gave it: “I am grateful to my teacher.”
Ask yourself one question before you choose. Am I talking about a person, or about a thing or a situation? The answer picks the preposition for you.
grammar.commonMistake: Both partners look right, so learners write “I am angry about my brother.” When you mean a person, use with: “I am angry with my brother.”
grammar.memoryTip: People take with and to. Things and situations take about and for. Picture a face for the first pair and an object for the second.

grammar.title: Adjectives That Do Not Need a Preposition
grammar.explanation: Position decides everything here. An adjective standing directly in front of its noun is already complete, so adding a preposition breaks the sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
In front of the noun, no preposition is needed: “The noble elder spoke wisely.”
In front of the noun again: “A misty morning greeted the village.”
After the verb, the preposition returns: “The father was proud of his son.”
Compare the two positions carefully.
Before the noun: “a proud father”.
After the verb: “The father was proud of his son.”
The same adjective behaves differently in the two places, so check where it is sitting before you reach for a preposition.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners sometimes add a linking word that is not wanted and write “The noble of elder spoke.” The adjective sits in front of the noun, so it stands alone: “The noble elder spoke.”
grammar.memoryTip: In front of the noun, the adjective is already home. After the verb it needs a bridge, and the preposition is that bridge.

grammar.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
grammar.explanation: Three errors cause nearly every problem with these pairs: choosing the wrong preposition, leaving it out, and adding one where none belongs.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Mistake 1. The wrong preposition.
“I am afraid from the dark.” becomes “I am afraid of the dark.”
“She is good in maths.” becomes “She is good at maths.”
“He was proud for his work.” becomes “He was proud of his work.”
Mistake 2. No preposition at all.
“She was proud her team.” becomes “She was proud of her team.”
“I am interested science.” becomes “I am interested in science.”
Mistake 3. One preposition too many.
“The noble of elder spoke.” becomes “The noble elder spoke.”
Read your sentence aloud once you have written it. The ear catches these three errors far faster than the eye does.
grammar.commonMistake: Excited slips most often, because “excited for” sounds natural when we speak. In writing, use “excited about the harvest festival.”
grammar.memoryTip: Fix in three sweeps. Is the preposition there? Is it the right one? Is it wanted at all?

grammar.title: Putting Adjective and Preposition Pairs into Practice
grammar.explanation: This last section brings the whole pattern together, moving from choosing a preposition to writing full sentences about your own life.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Work through the parts in order, because each one asks a little more of you than the last.
Part A gives you the sentence and asks only for the missing preposition.
Part B gives you the adjective and asks you to remember its partner.
Part C gives you the pair and asks you to finish the idea.
Part D gives you nothing but the pair, so the whole sentence is yours.
Keep the list of fifteen pairs from earlier in this unit beside you until the partners feel automatic.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often finish the last part with the same idea five times over. Change the subject of every sentence, so each one teaches you something new.
grammar.memoryTip: Test yourself the fast way. Cover the preposition column, read the adjective, and say its partner out loud before you look.

writing.title: Writing 1: Plan Your Own Fable
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Before you write a single sentence, plan your fable with the frame below. Notes are enough here, not full sentences.
Title: what will your fable be called?
Setting: where and when does it happen? A village, a river, a market, a farm or a forest all work well.
Characters: choose two or three animals. Give each one a name and a single strong quality.
Problem: what goes wrong? A drought, a lost tool, a broken bridge or a quarrel between neighbours.
Events: how do the characters try to solve it, and what goes wrong along the way?
Ending: how is the problem solved, and what does each character learn?
Moral: write the lesson in one clear sentence.
writing.modelText: Title: The Goat and the Weaver Bird. Setting: a dry riverbed at the edge of a farm. Characters: a boastful goat and a patient weaver bird. Problem: the last waterhole dries up. Events: the goat digs and gives up, while the bird watches where the ants are going. Ending: the ants lead both animals to a spring. Moral: patience notices what haste walks straight past.

items: Title: The Parrot and the Well
Setting: an orchard beside a well, during the hottest week of the dry season
Characters: a chattering parrot who loves the sound of his own voice, and a quiet, hardworking mole
Problem: the well's rope snaps and the bucket falls into the dark water below
Events: the parrot squawks instructions from his branch but never moves to help, while the mole tunnels beneath the well wall and pushes the bucket back up through a gap she opens
Ending: the orchard animals thank the mole, and the parrot goes strangely quiet once his advice has made no difference at all
Moral: one quiet helper can outshine ten loud advisers
otherAnswers: A different animal pair and problem would work just as well — for example a boastful rooster and a patient beetle solving a blocked irrigation channel.
The moral can be phrased differently as long as it captures the same lesson, such as: actions help more than advice.

writing.successCriteria: I chose a title; I named a setting; I gave each animal one strong quality; I wrote the problem in a single line; I wrote the moral in one clear sentence.
writing.support: Borrow the shape of “The Camel and the Sparrow” and change the animals and the problem.
writing.extension: Add a third animal and decide what that character adds to the lesson.

writing.title: Writing 2: Draft Your Fable
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write your fable now, using the plan you made. Aim for 150 to 200 words and finish with the moral on its own line.
Start with the setting and use adjectives to paint the picture for your reader.
Introduce the characters and what they are like. This is a good place for an adjective and preposition pair.
Create the problem, then show how the characters respond. Use speech marks so that we hear them talk.
End with the moral, stated plainly in one sentence.
writing.modelText: In a quiet forest beside a shining river lived a patient tortoise. He was proud of his slow, steady walk, and he was kind to every creature he met. One day a fierce storm washed the bridge away, and nobody could cross the water. “We must find another way over,” said the tortoise thoughtfully. He led the animals to a fallen log upstream, and by evening every one of them had crossed. Moral: patience and teamwork solve even the biggest problems.

items: Beside a dusty well at the edge of a fruit orchard, the ground was cracked and the air shimmered with heat.
There lived a chattering parrot who loved the sound of his own voice, and a small, hardworking mole who almost never spoke at all.

One scorching afternoon the old rope frayed and snapped, dropping the bucket into the dark water below. "You must fetch a hook and a long stick this instant!" squawked the parrot loudly from his branch, though he did not move an inch to help. The mole said nothing at all. She simply began digging beneath the well's stone wall until she found a narrow gap, and by evening she had pushed the bucket back up into the sunlight.
Moral: advice costs nothing, but quiet work is worth everything.

writing.successCriteria: I used my plan; my animals talk and act like people; the story has a beginning, a middle and an ending; I used speech marks for dialogue; I wrote the moral at the end.
writing.support: Say each sentence aloud before you write it, and keep your plan open beside the page.
writing.extension: Add one sentence of description that appeals to sound rather than sight.

Have I used at least two adjective and preposition pairs?

writing.title: Writing 4: The Fable from Jamal's Point of View
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Rewrite “The Camel and the Sparrow” as though Jamal is telling it himself. Use I, me and my throughout.
Start at the moment the sandstorm ends and finish just after Jamal apologises.
Show what Jamal is thinking when he laughs at Zara, not only what he says out loud.
Explain, in his voice, what changes his mind that evening.
Write three paragraphs and keep the moral, although Jamal now states it in his own words.
writing.modelText: I was the strongest animal in the village, and I was proud of it. When the little sparrow offered to help, I laughed, because I could not imagine what a bird that size could carry. By evening I understood that I had been measuring help in kilograms, and that was entirely the wrong measure.
writing.sentenceStarter: I was the strongest animal in...

items: Paragraph 1 (sandstorm ends, Jamal laughs at Zara): When the sandstorm finally died down, I shook the sand from my hump and looked at the wrecked well, certain that only I was strong enough to fix it. Zara the sparrow fluttered down and offered to help carry pebbles to clear the blocked spout, and I let out a great laugh, unable to picture what her tiny claws could possibly lift.

Paragraph 2 (what changes his mind): I spent the whole morning heaving boulders aside with barely a dent to show for it, while Zara flew back and forth without resting, dropping pebble after pebble into the narrow gaps my hooves could never reach. By midday the water was trickling through again, and I realised her small, steady trips had cleared what my great strength alone could not.

Paragraph 3 (apology and moral, in his own words): That evening I found Zara resting on the well's rim and told her I was sorry for laughing at her offer. I said that help is not measured by size but by whether it is given at all, and that I had judged her wrongly because I judged her only by her weight.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote in the first person all the way through; I showed Jamal's thoughts; I explained what changed his mind; I kept the moral in his own words; I checked my tenses.
writing.support: Underline three lines of the fable that Jamal saw for himself, and start from those.
writing.extension: Add one sentence in which Jamal admits something he would rather not say.

writing.title: Writing 5: Adjective and Preposition Sentences About Your Life
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write one full sentence for each pair below, and make every sentence true about you, your family or your community.
proud of
anxious about
interested in
grateful for
kind to
responsible for
afraid of
sorry for
Underline the adjective and circle the preposition in each finished sentence.
writing.modelText: I am proud of the vegetable patch that my grandmother and I planted behind our house. I am grateful for the neighbours who watered it while we were away. I am responsible for pulling the weeds out every Saturday morning.

items: I am proud of the mural our class painted for the school gate.
I am anxious about my long-distance race on Friday, because I have never run that far before.
I am interested in how bridges stay standing during a storm.
I am grateful for my older cousin, who taught me how to swim last summer.
My little brother is kind to our cat, even when she scratches him by accident.
I am responsible for feeding the chickens every evening before dinner.
I am afraid of the dark cellar under our house, so I always take a torch.
I was sorry for forgetting my friend's birthday, so I baked her a cake the next day.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote eight sentences; every sentence is true about my own life; each pair is used once; I underlined the adjective; I circled the preposition.
writing.support: Say the pair aloud first, then finish the sentence with the first true idea that comes to you.
writing.extension: Rewrite two of your sentences so that they begin with the person rather than with I.

writing.title: Writing 6: A Folklore Fact File
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short fact file about storytelling traditions around the world for a younger reader.
Use a heading, then one short paragraph for each tradition: Somali sheeko, Aesop's fables, Anansi tales and the Panchatantra.
Give every paragraph one fact and one example, and keep your sentences clear rather than long.
Finish with a single sentence that says what all four traditions share.
This is non-fiction, so check every fact against the reading before you hand it in.
writing.modelText: Anansi tales. Anansi is a spider who appears in stories told across West Africa and the Caribbean. He is clever rather than strong, and he usually talks his way out of trouble that he caused himself. Children learn from Anansi that cleverness has limits, because his tricks often catch him in the end.
writing.expectedLength: Four short paragraphs and a closing sentence

items: Heading: Storytelling Traditions Around the World

Somali sheeko: sheeko are stories told aloud in Somali communities, often in the evening, and passed from grandparents to children without ever being written down. Many sheeko explain why an animal looks or behaves the way it does, such as why the hyena laughs.

Aesop's fables: these short tales were told in Ancient Greece and are credited to a storyteller named Aesop. Each fable uses talking animals, such as the tortoise and the hare, to teach a lesson in only a few lines.
Anansi tales: Anansi is a clever spider who appears in stories from West Africa and the Caribbean. He usually solves problems by outwitting bigger, stronger animals rather than by fighting them.

Panchatantra: the Panchatantra is a very old collection of animal fables from India, first written to teach young princes how to make wise decisions. Its stories are grouped into five books, each teaching a different kind of wisdom.
Closing sentence: although these traditions come from different parts of the world, every one of them uses an animal character to teach a lesson that people still find useful today.

writing.successCriteria: I used a heading; I wrote one paragraph for each tradition; every paragraph has a fact and an example; my closing sentence names what they share; I checked each fact against the reading.
writing.support: Reread “Folklore Around the World” and highlight one fact per tradition before you start.
writing.extension: Add a short glossary explaining sheeko and folklore for your younger reader.

teacherNotes.note: Read the fable aloud before learners read it themselves, because the moral lands harder when the class hears the elder's speech performed. Pre-teach rubble, survival, residence and anxiety, since all four carry the courthouse story. Offer the comprehension answers orally to learners who write slowly, and accept a labelled drawing for the planning frame. For every task that uses a device, keep an adult in the room and never leave a learner alone with the AI tutor.

The unit source suggests four points where an AI tutor helps most, and each one needs an adult sitting with the learner. First, vocabulary: ask the tutor to explain a word simply, use it in three sentences, or give the opposite of rural. Second, comprehension: ask what figurative language means, or which clues show how Zara is feeling. Third, grammar: ask the tutor to check the learner's adjective and preposition sentences and to set five more. Fourth, writing: ask whether the fable has a clear moral, whether the dialogue is punctuated correctly, and how the opening could be sharper. Remind learners that the tutor guides them and the answers must stay in their own words.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The pairs are 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a, 5-f, 6-e, 7-h and 8-g. Learners most often swap survival and anxiety, so ask them to reread both meanings aloud before correcting.
The gaps read misty, nutrition, rural, pouch, encounter, regions, urban and coal. Gap 3 is the one to watch: learners who write urban have read the sentence about shops and hospitals backwards.

Answers will vary. Award the mark when the sentence reaches eight words and the word keeps its unit meaning. Watch shuffle, where a learner may use only the card meaning, and contain, which is often replaced by have.

The opposites are rural to urban, artificial to natural, urban to rural, and noble to selfish or dishonest. Accept greedy or cruel for noble, and accept real for artificial only if the learner explains the difference.

Twenty unit words appear across the two story parts: rubble, residence, regions, ancestor, role, misty, rumble, anxiety, continental, silvery, urban, nutrition, artificial, survival, coal, rural, noble, pouch, shuffle and encounter. Twelve is a pass and fifteen is strong.

Region means the shared area of dry land near the village. Ancestors are the villagers of earlier generations. Rumbled describes the long low noise the sandstorm made. Rubble is what the fallen walls became. Survival explains why the village needed the stream. Anxiety is Zara's worried feeling after Jamal laughs at her.
The answer is of. Proud is one of the pairs on the reference list, and learners who pick for have carried across the pattern from sorry for.
The answer is rubble. If a learner picks species, send them back to the sentence about the courthouse, where rubble is what surrounds the building.
The answer is the hidden stream behind the ridge. The lorry and the courthouse belong to the other story, which is a useful reminder to check which text a question names.
The answer is that no contribution is too small. Learners who choose hard work beats clever thinking have reversed the fable, because the sparrow's noticing is what saves the village.
The answer is the sentence about the trip. Ask learners to correct the other three aloud: good at maths, afraid of the dark corridor, interested in science.
The answer is related to a city or town. Rural is the opposite and is the distractor most often chosen, so pair the two words in the review.
The answer is on. Keen is the only pair on the list that takes on, so it is worth learning as a one-off rather than by rule.
The answer is the lorry passing the damaged road. Learners who choose another earthquake have recorded Amal's fear rather than what the passage says actually happened.
The answer is the Anansi tales. Use the miss to revisit the definition: folklore is passed down and retold, while a timetable or a shopping list is written once for a single purpose.
The answer is one clear problem and a short plot. The other options describe novels and fairy tales, which is exactly the contrast the first reading draws.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "There’s a Lesson in That" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 9-10 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'coal'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Read a fable closely and state its moral in your own words.
Identify the features of fables and folklore, including animal characters and a stated moral.
Use adjective and preposition pairs accurately in speech and in writing.
Use the twenty-five unit words accurately in sentences of your own.
Plan, draft and revise an original fable with a clear beginning, middle and ending.
Discuss stories with others, build on what they say and disagree respectfully.
Tell literal language apart from figurative language and explain the picture it creates.
Explain why a character behaves as they do, using evidence from the text.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "What Makes a Fable?" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Camel and the Sparrow" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "What Are Adjectives + Prepositions?" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
items: Jamal was proud of his own strength.
Amal was anxious about the journey.
She was angry with her friend.
The noble elder spoke wisely.
I am afraid of the dark.
Work through the parts in order, because each one asks a little more of you than the last.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: A written moral for “The Camel and the Sparrow” plus four accurate comprehension answers about that fable.
A completed feature checklist for the fable and a folklore fact file covering four traditions.
Grammar Parts A to D completed with fewer than three preposition errors, plus two accurate pairs inside the drafted fable.
Activities 1 to 4 marked correct and eight original sentences of at least eight words each.
A planning frame, a draft of 150 to 200 words and a revised final copy carrying the moral on its own line.
A recorded discussion in which the learner asks one question, adds to one point and gives one reasoned disagreement.
A written explanation of “Even the smallest raindrop helps to fill the river” that names it as figurative and unpacks the image.
A paragraph on why Jamal changes his mind, quoting two lines from the fable, plus a retelling in his voice.
